newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US '97 trade gap to widen as exports slow.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US '97 trade gap to widen as exports slow.

text.p: The U.S. international trade deficit will widen this year as the dollar's recent strength and expected economic weakness overseas restricts exports, said economists polled by Reuters.

The Reuters quarterly economic survey showed average expectations that the U.S. trade gap would widen from a $32.28 billion shortfall in the first quarter of 1997 to a $32.87 deficit in the third quarter. A mild rebound to a $32.30 gap was seen in the final quarter of 1997.
While steady economic conditions in the U.S. may spur the production of more goods for export, economists said foreign buyers could be in short supply.

"I don't think we will export a heck of a lot more to Western Europe, Japan or Asia. Economies there consistently have come in under expectations for domestic growth," said Nancy Kimelman, chief economist at Technical Data.
"It's one thing to say the U.S. will want to export more, but that's not really the issue. The issue is, who will buy it?" she queried.
The dollar's recent surge against most major currencies to its highest level in years could boost U.S. imports and strangle exports come the second half, economists said.

A pronounced lag, ranging from one to two years, typically occurs between a rise in currency rates and its eventual impact on shipments of exports and imports, due to the prevalence of long-term industry contracts and the complications involved in changes of demand and distribution.
But historical data show a stronger currency eventually hurts the balance of trade by making imports cheaper and exports more expensive for foreign buyers, economists said.
The dollar has already risen about 51 percent versus the yen and 23 percent against the mark since its long-term rally from post-World War II lows began in March and April 1995.
However, these gains have yet to make a significant dent in overall U.S. exports, analysts said.

"The rise in the dollar is certainly giving some pricing headaches to exporters, but in general they do not seem to be suggesting, in anything like the vocal way they did in the early '80s, that they are hurting," said David Munro, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics.
In fact, the latest U.S. trade data showed a deceleration of the U.S. trade deficit for a second straight month.

The trade gap rose to $8.4 billion in November, undercutting Wall Street expectations for a $9.8 billion showing. This came on the heels of an impressive $8.01 billion shortfall in October, well below the typical $11 billion deficit seen in months prior.
"Companies are looking to export growth as a means to bolster production, but at the same time, they are fighting a headwind now, which is the dollar," Kimelman said.
"I see the two obviously working against each other."

The Reuters poll of 17 economists, conducted Tuesday through Thursday of last week, also showed the dollar's rise peaking in the first quarter of 1997 against the yen and mark, which could mitigate its effect on trade, analysts said.
However, the greenback's performance on a trade-weighted basis may differ as many of the large U.S. business partners are located in the Americas.
A few economists foresaw the October and November improvement in trade continuing throughout the year. These predictions were heavily dependent on strong performance by overseas economies.

"It's my guess foreign economies will grow slightly faster in 1997 than they did in the prior year and that the U.S. economy will slow down, especially by the second half," said Richard Rippe, senior vice president and chief economist at Prudential Securities Inc.
"So we won't be pulling in imports quite as fast and export growth will be fueled by foreign demand," said Rippe, who forecast the U.S. trade deficit would narrow to $24.75 billion by year-end.
